title: Hybrid Cross-Modal Attention Network for Early Breast Cancer Detection in Low-Resource Clinical Settings
authors: Simon Hadush Nrea, Filimon Gidey Gebremichael, Gebrekirstos Hagos Gebrekirstos, Yaecob Girmay Gezahegn
abstract: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women in Sub-Saharan Africa, where delayed diagnosis results from limited radiology expertise and fragmented clinical data systems. Although deep learning models have demonstrated strong performance in mammographic analysis, most rely solely on imaging data and are trained on Western populations, limiting their applicability in African healthcare settings. This paper presents a Hybrid Cross-Modal Attention Network (HCMAN) that integrates mammogram images with structured clinical data using transformer-based cross-modal attention mechanisms. The model was developed and validated using a locally collected dataset of 2,560 mammogram images from 1,024 patients across four Ethiopian referral hospitals, with biopsy-confirmed ground truth labels. The proposed framework achieves 97.8% accuracy, 97.2% sensitivity, 98.3% specificity, and an AUC of 0.987, significantly outperforming image-only baselines. The system demonstrates robustness to low-quality images typical of resource-limited settings, with only 3.2% performance degradation compared to 8.7% for image-only models. Cross-modal attention analysis reveals clinically appropriate behavior: higher reliance on clinical features for ambiguous cases such as dense breasts and young patients. The model's lightweight architecture enables deployment on standard hospital workstations (<2 seconds inference on CPU). This work advances sustainable, context-aware AI solutions for equitable breast cancer diagnostics in Africa.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid AI model that combines mammogram images with patient clinical data can improve early breast cancer detection in low-resource settings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach may support more accurate and context-aware breast cancer screening in settings with limited radiology expertise and fragmented records.
method: Transformer-based cross-modal attention fused mammogram and structured clinical data
Trained and validated on 2,560 mammograms from 1,024 patients across four Ethiopian referral hospitals
Compared against image-only baselines and assessed robustness on low-quality images
infographic.evidence_signal: The model achieved 97.8% accuracy, 97.2% sensitivity, 98.3% specificity, and an AUC of 0.987, with biopsy-confirmed labels and only 3.2% performance degradation on poor-quality images.
infographic.watch_item: Real-world deployment may require careful local validation to confirm performance across different populations, workflows, and data quality conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Hybrid Cross-Modal Attention Network for Early Breast Cancer Detection in Low-Resource Clinical Settings

title: Bridging Human and Model Attention: Explainability Analysis of CNN, Mamba, and ViT Architectures with Gaze-Based Validation
authors: Marco Stefani, Edoardo Parpaiola, Matteo Bino, Gianluca Caregnato, Francesco Roncolato, Daniel Fusaro
abstract: High-risk applications of deep learning require precise characterization of model decision-making. We conduct a systematic explainability evaluation across Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Vision Transformers (ViTs), and Vision Mamba (ViM). Unlike predominantly qualitative studies, we quantify the alignment between model attention and human visual perception using eye-tracking ground truth. We formalize this comparison via a standardized normalization pipeline mapping post-hoc attribution maps and gaze heatmaps onto spatial probability distributions. Alignment is evaluated across fine-grained classification, medical imaging, and emotion recognition using architecture-specific XAI methods. We measure fidelity using Jensen-Shannon similarity, Chi-square similarity, and Pearson correlation, three complementary estimators capturing support overlap, mass discrepancy, and structural co-variation. Our results reveal distinct attention dynamics: CNNs tend to exhibit a more global focus, with spatially more diffuse saliency maps that correlate well with human perception in general contexts, while ViTs demonstrate fine-grained, patch-level attention, often focused on discriminative microfeatures. The Mamba architecture shows biased behavior: it achieves strong explainability in medical tasks but exhibits divergent intensity distributions in natural images; our analytical characterization of the metrics makes this dissociation explicit, since near-unit support overlap is attained simultaneously with a vanishing linear correlation. We further analyze the effect of backbone freezing and ensemble strategies on model interpretability. The results highlight how architectural and training choices influence the alignment between model saliency and human visual attention.

infographic.key_insight: CNNs, ViTs, and Vision Mamba show different attention patterns, and their saliency alignment with human gaze varies by task and architecture.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Understanding which model attention better matches human visual focus can improve trust and interpretability in medical imaging AI, especially for high-stakes decisions.
method: Compared CNN, ViT, and Vision Mamba architectures across fine-grained classification, medical imaging, and emotion recognition.
Mapped post-hoc attribution maps and eye-tracking heatmaps into standardized spatial probability distributions.
Evaluated alignment using Jensen-Shannon similarity, Chi-square similarity, and Pearson correlation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports gaze-based validation across multiple datasets/tasks, revealing strong task-dependent alignment differences and cases where support overlap is high but linear correlation is low.
infographic.watch_item: Attention alignment metrics can disagree with each other, so high overlap does not necessarily mean the model matches human visual behavior in a meaningful way.
infographic.paper_title: Bridging Human and Model Attention: Explainability Analysis of CNN, Mamba, and ViT Architectures with Gaze-Based Validation

title: Coverage-Aware Reasoning with Medical Tokens for Diagnosis Prediction
authors: Kaisong Zhang, Haotian Fang, Junmeng Zhou, Hang Lv, Yulan Pan, Yanchao Tan
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer promising potential for next-visit diagnosis prediction, owing to their ability to integrate longitudinal clinical evidence and reason over it in natural language. However, reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning commonly rewards each trajectory according to the correctness of its final answer. In next-visit diagnosis prediction, multiple diagnoses can be simultaneously valid, but independently rewarding one diagnosis per trajectory does not distinguish repeated hits from coverage of different diagnoses. The policy can therefore concentrate on a few correct diagnoses, leaving others uncovered. Meanwhile, LLM tokenizers can split ICD codes into several generic tokens with limited clinical meaning, requiring multiple decoding steps to predict each diagnosis and hindering reasoning over a large disease vocabulary. To address both challenges, we propose CARing, a framework that represents diagnoses with compositional Semantic IDs (SIDs) and optimizes reasoning trajectories for multi-label coverage. Concretely, we first encode ontology-enriched disease semantics into compact SIDs through residual quantization, and ground the resulting SID tokens in natural language and longitudinal EHR contexts through multi-task alignment and reasoning-enriched training to unlock transferable LLM reasoning. CARing further improves unordered multi-label prediction through a coverage reward for reinforcement learning and multi-positive supervision. At inference time, the model supports both efficient direct constrained decoding and multi-chain reasoning with rank fusion. On MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, CARing exceeds all EHR-trained baselines in weighted F1 and attains the highest top-k recall at every reported cutoff, including R@30 of 46.04% and 46.52% in reasoning mode. Our codes and logs are available at https://github.com/zmlxzyh/CARing-Codes-Logs.

infographic.key_insight: CARing improves next-visit diagnosis prediction by pairing compact medical token representations with a coverage-based reward so the model learns to cover multiple valid diagnoses, not just repeat a few easy ones.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help clinical NLP systems produce more complete differential diagnosis predictions from longitudinal EHRs, especially in multi-label settings where several diagnoses may be correct at once.
method: Represents diagnoses as compact Semantic IDs (SIDs) learned from ontology-enriched disease semantics via residual quantization.
Aligns SID tokens with natural language and EHR context using multi-task alignment and reasoning-enriched training.
Uses coverage reward plus multi-positive supervision, with direct constrained decoding or multi-chain reasoning at inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, the method outperformed EHR-trained baselines in weighted F1 and achieved the best top-k recall at all reported cutoffs, including R@30 of 46.04% and 46.52% in reasoning mode.
infographic.watch_item: Because the approach depends on learned SID vocabularies, constrained decoding, and EHR-specific training data, performance may be sensitive to ontology quality and integration into real clinical workflows.
infographic.paper_title: Coverage-Aware Reasoning with Medical Tokens for Diagnosis Prediction

title: Frozen Models, Evolving Expertise: Model-Agnostic Learning from Deployment Experience for Multimodal Medical AI
authors: Yexiao He, Yucheng Tang, Pengfei Guo, Yufan He, Andriy Myronenko, Can Zhao
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) are usually frozen after deployment, so they do not learn from the cases they solve. This is especially concerning in medicine, where new clinical evidence, updated guidelines, and new therapies can change established practice. Fine-tuning can update the model, but it requires access to model weights and additional training. Parameter-free methods avoid training, but they may overfit a fixed validation set, lack reliable domain knowledge, or lose visual details by saving experience only as text. To address these limitations, we present a model-agnostic framework that allows frozen LLMs and VLMs to learn from deployment experience through three forms of external expertise: a Skill that guides reasoning and tool use, a Knowledge Memory that stores reliable facts supported by earlier cases or trusted external evidence, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base that keeps visual examples and guides the model to relate each retrieved case to the current image. Instead of relying on a fixed validation set, a validation strategy keeps an update only if it helps on new cases without degrading performance on earlier ones. Across six benchmarks covering clinical diagnosis, clinical workflows, medical reasoning, and medical and non-medical visual reasoning, and with four open-weight and closed-source base models, our framework improves performance during online deployment by up to 34.2% over the base model on medical tasks, generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without further optimization, and works in non-medical domains.

infographic.key_insight: Frozen medical LLMs/VLMs can keep improving after deployment by learning from past cases through external skill, knowledge, and multimodal memory rather than by retraining model weights.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help clinical AI stay closer to evolving evidence and workflows while preserving visual details important for diagnosis and decision support.
method: Adds a learned Skill to guide reasoning and tool use.
Stores trusted case-based facts in a Knowledge Memory.
Keeps a Multimodal Knowledge Base of visual examples and uses a validation rule that only accepts updates that help new cases without hurting prior performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on six benchmarks across clinical diagnosis, workflows, reasoning, and visual reasoning with four base models, showing up to 34.2% improvement during online deployment.
infographic.watch_item: Because updates depend on external memories and online validation, deployment quality may still hinge on the reliability, coverage, and maintenance of stored cases and evidence.
infographic.paper_title: Frozen Models, Evolving Expertise: Model-Agnostic Learning from Deployment Experience for Multimodal Medical AI

title: ECGWmark: Deep Watermarking for Electrocardiogram Signals
authors: Kuan-Yu Chen, Kuan-Chen Wang, Yu Tsao, Jian-Jiun Ding
abstract: Secure transmission of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals remains a major challenge in telecardiology. While traditional mathematical watermarking can embed patient metadata directly into ECG signals, it is highly fragile against temporal desynchronization such as circular phase shifts. In contrast, existing deep watermarking approaches for temporal signals, such as audio, typically rely on lossy quantization, which compromises the high-frequency micro-morphological details critical for clinical diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we propose ECGWmark, a fully convolutional and quantization-free deep watermarking framework for medical time-series. ECGWmark operates in a continuous, full-resolution latent space and utilizes a localized frame-level mechanism to improve the robustness to severe desynchronization. Crucially, we introduce a differentiable Physiological Loss guided by a clinical classifier to preserve diagnostic semantics. Experiments on the benchmark MIT-BIH database show that ECGWmark maintains channel-bit extraction accuracy above 90% under the evaluated circular temporal shifts. Furthermore, under a rigorous inter-patient diagnostic evaluation, Class-V sensitivity changes from 71.97% to 76.50%, whereas Macro-F1 changes from 35.25% to 34.71% and Class-S sensitivity from 8.89% to 1.39%; these results indicate mixed class-level effects.

infographic.key_insight: ECGWmark is a fully convolutional, quantization-free watermarking method that embeds data in ECG signals while aiming to preserve diagnostic detail and resist temporal misalignment.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It could support safer ECG data transmission in telecardiology by protecting patient metadata without heavily degrading waveform features used for diagnosis.
method: Uses a continuous, full-resolution latent space instead of lossy quantization.
Adds a localized frame-level design to improve robustness to circular phase shifts and other desynchronization.
Includes a differentiable Physiological Loss guided by a clinical classifier to preserve medical semantics.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the MIT-BIH database, the model kept channel-bit extraction accuracy above 90% under tested circular temporal shifts, with mixed effects in inter-patient diagnostic metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The reported class-level diagnostic changes are uneven, so clinical deployment would need careful validation to ensure watermarking does not alter performance across rhythm classes.
infographic.paper_title: ECGWmark: Deep Watermarking for Electrocardiogram Signals

title: EchoTab: Learning Measurement-Grounded Representations for Echocardiographic Diagnosis through Tabular Reconstruction
authors: Michelle Espranita Liman, Ioana Ionac, Alexander Müller, Eimo Martens, Daniel Rueckert, Philip Müller
abstract: Diagnostic information in multi-view medical imaging studies, like echocardiography, is distributed across views, each capturing different aspects of cardiac structure and function. In clinical practice, these views are first interpreted through quantitative measurements, which then support specific diagnoses. However, existing echo representation learning methods do not explicitly model measurements as an intermediate representation between views and diagnosis. As a result, individual measurements are not explicitly represented in a form that downstream diagnostic tasks can selectively use, hindering accurate diagnosis. Inspired by this hierarchical clinical workflow, we introduce EchoTab, a measurement-grounded representation learning framework that represents multi-view echocardiography studies using measurement-specific tokens as an intermediate representation between echo views and diagnosis. Each measurement token selectively attends to the views relevant to its estimation and is trained through tabular reconstruction to predict the corresponding measurement value. The resulting tokens form a factorized echo representation, which encode clinically meaningful structural and functional properties and can be selectively used for downstream diagnosis. Unlike the commonly used contrastive approaches, EchoTab does not require negative samples or large batch sizes. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate that EchoTab learns effective measurement-grounded representations that improve diagnosis classification in multi-view echocardiography and its learned attention aligns with established measurement-view relationships used by cardiologists. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/michelleespranita/EchoTab.

infographic.key_insight: EchoTab learns measurement-specific tokens from multi-view echocardiography, using tabular reconstruction to create clinically meaningful intermediate representations before diagnosis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: By grounding representations in standard echocardiographic measurements, the approach can improve diagnostic classification while aligning with how clinicians interpret echo studies.
method: Measurement tokens each attend to the echo views relevant to a specific cardiac measurement.
Tokens are trained with tabular reconstruction to predict measurement values.
The resulting factorized representation is then used for downstream diagnosis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments on two datasets showing improved diagnosis classification and attention patterns that match established measurement-view relationships.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the availability and quality of measurement labels, and real-world integration will need validation across broader echo workflows and sites.
infographic.paper_title: EchoTab: Learning Measurement-Grounded Representations for Echocardiographic Diagnosis through Tabular Reconstruction

title: Tensor-based Fusion of Multi-modal Data for Predicting Cancer Risk Levels
authors: Ali Anaissi, Yuanzhe Jia, Qishun Peng, Weidong Huang, Ali Braytee, Junaid Akram
abstract: Cancer diagnosis and treatment increasingly rely on multi-modal diagnostic technologies that generate high-dimensional datasets. Although these datasets are rich in pathological information, they pose considerable challenges in interpretation, dimensionality reduction, and clinical applicability. Conventional machine learning approaches often fail to extract meaningful cross-modal features, thereby limiting predictive accuracy in patient risk stratification. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an unsupervised machine learning framework that integrates feature extraction, tensor decomposition, and clustering to improve cancer risk prediction. The framework employs tensor decomposition to fuse heterogeneous genomic and clinical data, enabling the extraction of latent, biologically meaningful features that outperform unimodal feature sets. Multiple feature extraction strategies are investigated, and the resulting features are subsequently clustered using a range of clustering algorithms. Comparative evaluations based on internal and external metrics are then used to identify the most effective configurations. The framework is validated on LinkedOmics data comprising 11,158 patients across 32 cancer types. For patient risk stratification, clinically relevant attributes such as tumor purity, pathological stage, and survival outcomes serve as ground-truth indicators. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of tSVD+GMM, which consistently outperforms other configurations across clinical benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: Tensor-based fusion of multi-modal genomic and clinical data can reveal latent features that improve cancer risk stratification over unimodal approaches.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach may help support more accurate patient risk grouping using routinely relevant markers such as tumor purity, stage, and survival outcomes.
method: Unsupervised framework combining feature extraction, tensor decomposition, and clustering
Fused heterogeneous genomic and clinical datasets into latent representations
Compared multiple feature-extraction and clustering combinations
infographic.evidence_signal: Validated on LinkedOmics with 11,158 patients across 32 cancer types, using internal/external clustering metrics and clinical benchmarks; tSVD+GMM performed best.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on retrospective multi-modal datasets and clustering benchmarks, so clinical deployment would need careful external validation and workflow integration.
infographic.paper_title: Tensor-based Fusion of Multi-modal Data for Predicting Cancer Risk Levels

title: A4-MR: Abnormality-aware Anatomical Alignment for MR
authors: Noel D'souza, Zhijian Yang, Nishank Singla, Pranay Doshi, Krisztian Koos, Fei Tan
abstract: Recent advances in large-scale foundation models have enabled strong generalization across a wide range of clinical and research tasks in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, existing vision-language MRI models remain limited in anatomy-specific localization and pathology-aware representation, particularly in real-world settings. We introduce A4-MR, a 3D vision-language foundation model trained on approximately 50,000 MRI studies comprising 491,000 series, roughly half of which are paired with radiology reports. A4-MR is designed to: (1) learn anatomy localization through large-scale pretraining with noisy labels; (2) align image and text representations at the anatomical level; and (3) learn distinct representations of healthy and abnormal anatomy. Across a diverse set of downstream tasks, A4-MR outperforms existing foundation models, including a +1.7 AUROC improvement over MedSigLIP for abnormality detection. Using a frozen encoder, A4-MR also surpasses an end-to-end task-specific MedNeXt model for knee segmentation by +1.4 Dice and performs comparably to the best task-specific model for abdominal organ segmentation on AMOS, within 0.4 Dice. Finally, without anatomical prompts, A4-MR localizes 3D anatomy comparably to MedSAM2 provided with ground-truth bounding boxes. Together, these results demonstrate that anatomy-level multimodal alignment and abnormality-aware representation learning can enable a single MRI foundation model to support localization, segmentation, and pathology-related tasks.

infographic.key_insight: A4-MR is a 3D MRI foundation model that aligns images and text at the anatomical level and learns separate representations for healthy and abnormal anatomy, improving localization, segmentation, and abnormality detection.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help build a single MRI model that supports anatomy localization and downstream tasks more robustly across real-world clinical cases, including pathology-aware applications.
method: Pretrained on ~50,000 MRI studies and 491,000 series, with about half paired to radiology reports.
Uses large-scale noisy labels to learn anatomy localization and anatomical image-text alignment.
Learns distinct healthy vs abnormal anatomy representations for pathology-aware modeling.
infographic.evidence_signal: In abstract-level evaluation, A4-MR outperformed prior foundation models, including +1.7 AUROC for abnormality detection, +1.4 Dice over MedNeXt for knee segmentation, and near-best performance on abdominal organ segmentation.
infographic.watch_item: Results are promising, but performance may depend on the quality and diversity of the pretraining data, and clinical deployment would still need external validation across sites, scanners, and MRI protocols.
infographic.paper_title: A4-MR: Abnormality-aware Anatomical Alignment for MR

title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
authors: Chandravardhan Singh Raghaw, Shahid Shafi Dar, Arnav Nishith Sharma, Shrey Modi, Nagendra Kumar
abstract: Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi-view information. We present Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation (CliQ-RRG), a unified two-stage framework for interpretable and clinically grounded reporting. In Stage 1, CliQ-RRG employs a Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment module that aligns image and text representations using predicted disease embeddings, reinforced by a Prior-Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to capture multi-view dependencies across current and prior scans. In Stage 2, GraphRAG-guided retrieval augments intermediate textual representations with graph-grounded clinical evidence, and a large language model restructures them into concise, interpretable question-answer (QA) pairs with diagnostic summaries. Experiments on two public chest X-ray benchmarks demonstrate that CliQ-RRG consistently outperforms prior methods across both lexical and clinical metrics, generating accurate and clinically coherent QA-style radiology reports. Code is available at: https://github.com/chandravardhan-singh-raghaw/CliQ-RRG.

infographic.key_insight: CliQ-RRG turns radiology report generation into a clinically guided, two-stage process that aligns images with disease-aware text signals and then rewrites them into concise QA-style reports.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach aims to produce more interpretable, clinically grounded chest X-ray reports that better capture diagnostic cues and multi-view context for radiology workflows.
method: Stage 1: Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment with predicted disease embeddings.
Stage 1: Prior-Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to model current and prior scan relationships.
Stage 2: GraphRAG-guided retrieval plus an LLM to convert intermediate text into QA pairs and diagnostic summaries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains over prior methods on two public chest X-ray benchmarks, improving both lexical and clinical evaluation metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on reliable disease prediction, retrieval quality, and benchmark-style evaluation; real-world deployment may be affected by domain shift and integration complexity.
infographic.paper_title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation

title: BioBigBird: A Sparse Attention Model for Long-Range Dependency Processing in Biomedical Text
authors: Roshan Balaji, Pavan Kumar S, Vasudev Gupta, Sreejith N, Keerthana Sridhar, Nirav Bhatt
abstract: While domain-specific Large Language Models (LLMs) have encoded vast biomedical knowledge, their limited context windows often hinder a deep understanding of nuanced relationships within and across texts. To address this limitation, we introduce BioBigBird, a bidirectional language model pre-trained on extensive biomedical literature and clinical data, specifically designed to handle long-range dependencies. BioBigBird leverages a sparse attention mechanism to process sequences up to 4096 tokens, and its training incorporates a multi-stage process to mitigate noise from the large-scale pre-training corpus. We further enhance its performance by employing a multi-task learning (MTL) framework that jointly optimizes for Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction. Comprehensive evaluations on the BLURB benchmark reveal that our MTL-enhanced BioBigBird achieves highly competitive results against state-of-the-art models. Our work contributes an effective methodology for developing powerful, long-context language models for specialized domains, demonstrating the value of extended sequence processing for complex text analysis. Our models are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/bisectgroup/biobigbird.

infographic.key_insight: BioBigBird extends biomedical text understanding by using sparse attention to capture long-range dependencies in sequences up to 4096 tokens.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could improve clinical NLP tasks that need context across long documents, such as entity recognition and relation extraction in biomedical literature and records.
method: Pre-trained a bidirectional biomedical language model on large-scale literature and clinical data.
Used sparse attention to support much longer input sequences than typical LLM context windows.
Added multi-task learning for Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive performance on the BLURB benchmark, with the MTL-enhanced BioBigBird achieving highly competitive results versus state-of-the-art models.
infographic.watch_item: Long-context models can be compute-intensive and their real-world performance may depend on data quality, preprocessing, and deployment constraints.
infographic.paper_title: BioBigBird: A Sparse Attention Model for Long-Range Dependency Processing in Biomedical Text

title: MedCORE: Criteria-Grounded Clinical Reasoning for Interpretable Medical Image Diagnosis
authors: Asim Khan, Samee Ullah Khan, Dwarikanath Mahapatra
abstract: Clinical diagnosis is inherently a structured reasoning process, yet existing deep learning models often bypass this structure by mapping image features directly to disease labels without explicitly interrogating the morphological and textural criteria that clinicians systematically evaluate. This limits diagnostic transparency and may compromise safe clinical deployment. We present MedCORE (Medical Criteria-Oriented Reasoning and Evidence), a structured diagnostic framework that operationalizes clinical reasoning within a vision-language architecture. For each input image, MedCORE decomposes the diagnostic process into clinically defined criteria, spatially localizes each criterion to diagnostically relevant image regions, encodes evidence through multi-scale representations that capture macro-structural and micro-textural pathological characteristics, and refines criterion representations using a Graph Attention Network that explicitly models inter-criteria dependencies. Criterion representations are further aligned with clinical text descriptors, reinforced through class-wise visual prototypes, and aggregated using uncertainty-calibrated weighting that proportionally discounts low-confidence diagnostic evidence. MedCORE is validated across three clinically heterogeneous imaging modalities, including dermoscopic lesion classification on ISIC 2018, breast ultrasound lesion characterization on BUSI, and diabetic retinopathy grading on IDRiD. Quantitatively, MedCORE achieves 89.2% accuracy, 85.7% macro-F1, and 96.4% AUC on ISIC 2018; 96.1% accuracy, 95.2% macro-F1, and 98.4% AUC on BUSI; and 84.3% accuracy, 80.2% macro-F1, and 92.8% AUC on IDRiD. These results demonstrate consistent improvements over strong CNN, transformer, biomedical vision-language, concept-based, and prototype-based baselines.

infographic.key_insight: MedCORE makes medical image diagnosis more interpretable by structuring predictions around explicit clinical criteria rather than direct image-to-label mapping.
infographic.clinical_relevance: By aligning image evidence with clinician-like reasoning and uncertainty-aware weighting, the approach could support safer, more transparent diagnostic decision support across multiple imaging tasks.
method: Decomposes each diagnosis into clinically defined criteria and localizes supporting image regions.
Uses multi-scale feature encoding plus a Graph Attention Network to model relationships among criteria.
Aligns criterion evidence with clinical text descriptors, visual prototypes, and uncertainty-calibrated aggregation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validated on ISIC 2018, BUSI, and IDRiD, with reported performance of 89.2%/85.7%/96.4% AUC, 96.1%/95.2%/98.4% AUC, and 84.3%/80.2%/92.8% AUC respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The framework’s added complexity may make real-world deployment dependent on high-quality criterion annotations, robust localization, and careful clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: MedCORE: Criteria-Grounded Clinical Reasoning for Interpretable Medical Image Diagnosis

title: Cite What You Explore: Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning over Medical KGs with Verifiable Evidence
authors: Chen Chen, Dongjie Wang, Mei Liu, Zijun Yao
abstract: Post-discharge risk prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) is difficult because many dependencies that link discharge-time observations to downstream complications, such as comorbidity cascades and drug-disease interactions, are absent from the record. External medical knowledge graphs (KGs) can supply these missing dependencies, but tracing them demands three properties: KG exploration must remain cost-bounded, retrieved evidence must be differentiated by source quality, and the resulting rationale must be citable for retrospective review. Large language models (LLMs) can plan and verify over structured evidence, making them natural candidates for KG reasoning, but existing LLM-based methods do not satisfy these three properties jointly. In this paper, we propose BAR, a Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning framework over medical KGs with three contributions. First, BAR refines the raw KG into disease-specific evidence graphs whose edges carry support scores and provenance records, turning the KG into a quality-annotated reasoning space rather than a static feature source. Second, an LLM then reasons over this graph through a plan-navigate-verify loop that decomposes the question into steps, retrieves evidence under a patient-specific budget, and revises when verification fails. Third, a reasoning policy is trained with a reward that compares predictions with and without acquired evidence, combined with acquisition cost and citation-integrity terms. Across 8 diseases and 3 prediction horizons on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, BAR improves AUPRC by 3.4 points over the strongest baseline, raises citation precision from 59.8% to 77.9%, and consumes only 62-65% of the budget cap.

infographic.key_insight: BAR helps an LLM make post-discharge risk predictions by exploring medical knowledge graphs in a budget-aware way and requiring evidence to be verifiable and citable.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could make EHR-based risk predictions more explainable for retrospective review by linking outputs to traceable medical knowledge rather than hidden model reasoning.
method: Builds disease-specific evidence graphs from medical KGs with support scores and provenance.
Uses a plan-navigate-verify LLM loop to retrieve evidence within a patient-specific budget and revise when verification fails.
Trains the reasoning policy with rewards for predictive gain, lower acquisition cost, and citation integrity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 8 diseases and 3 prediction horizons on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, BAR improved AUPRC by 3.4 points over the strongest baseline, raised citation precision from 59.8% to 77.9%, and used 62-65% of the budget cap.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and citation quality depend on KG coverage, provenance quality, and careful budget tuning, so real-world deployment may need validation on local data.
infographic.paper_title: Cite What You Explore: Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning over Medical KGs with Verifiable Evidence

title: Learning Features, Not Layouts: Feature-Axis Attention as a Transfer Prior for Medical Imaging
authors: Aon Safdar, Mohamed Saadeldin
abstract: Natural-image-pretrained foundation models are increasingly adapted to medical imaging, yet transfer remains unreliable under domain shift, modality heterogeneity, and label scarcity. We trace part of this fragility to an overlooked design choice. Standard vision transformers place all global modeling on self-attention over spatial tokens, an object-layout prior well suited to natural scenes but not to medical images, where the discriminative signal lies in feature correlations and texture that recur across scanners while layout does not. We ask whether the axis of global attention, spatial versus feature, is itself a lever for transferable medical representations. Existing channel-aware hybrids confound this question, adding channel attention to a spatially-mixed backbone and leaving the axes coupled and the feature axis unmeasurable in isolation. We design FAD-ViT, a backbone that strictly decouples the two axes, making feature-axis attention the primary global operator and the attention axis a controlled variable. Evaluating comprehensively across 23 classification, segmentation, and low-data tasks under matched tokenization, capacity, and protocol, we find that shifting global attention from the spatial to the feature axis leaves from-scratch performance essentially unchanged, yet markedly strengthens transfer. Identical ImageNet pretraining yields up to roughly three times the transfer gain, with consistent improvements on every held-out segmentation task at up to a quarter the parameter count and far lower compute than standard and channel-attention baselines. The advantage is largest where texture rather than geometry is discriminative, tracking greater reuse of pretrained features. The axis of global attention is thus a design lever for medical transfer, and making it channel-primary is a simple, cheap, and principled choice.

infographic.key_insight: For medical imaging transfer, making global attention operate across features/channels instead of spatial layout can preserve from-scratch performance while substantially improving reuse of pretrained representations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could make foundation models more reliable and compute-efficient for medical image tasks where texture and feature correlations matter more than object geometry.
method: Built FAD-ViT, a vision transformer that strictly decouples spatial and feature axes.
Made feature-axis attention the primary global operator and kept the attention axis controlled.
Compared against standard and channel-attention baselines under matched tokenization, capacity, and training protocol.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 23 classification, segmentation, and low-data tasks, feature-axis attention produced stronger transfer, with up to about 3x the transfer gain and consistent segmentation improvements under identical ImageNet pretraining.
infographic.watch_item: The approach was evaluated under controlled benchmarking, so real-world gains may depend on task type, scanner variability, and how faithfully the feature-axis design is implemented.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Features, Not Layouts: Feature-Axis Attention as a Transfer Prior for Medical Imaging

title: Evidence-Bound Reasoning: Neuro-Semantic Verification of Biomedical AI in Glioblastoma Radiogenomics
authors: Mariya Miteva, Maria Nisheva-Pavlova
abstract: Background: Biomedical AI can generate plausible explanations without reliably verifying whether each statement is supported by patient-specific evidence. We developed a neuro-semantic verification framework that converts radiomic measurements into addressable evidence records and machine-checkable claims. Methods: UPenn-GBM radiomics were aligned with de novo CaPTk extraction from standardized MRI and expert-validated segmentations in an independent multicenter cohort. The shared space comprised 1,728 features from T1, T1GD, T2, and FLAIR MRI across three tumor regions. Reference-defined semantic states were derived from 611 UPenn cases. We evaluated cross-cohort transportability, model-linked provenance, deterministic verification, controlled predictive degradation, and an LLM claim-extraction pilot; MGMT prediction served only as a transport stress test. Results: Median semantic-state agreement was 0.786 (weighted kappa 0.709), ranging from 0.918 for morphologic to 0.252 for intensity features. The external evidence ledger contained 1,655 model-linked records for 331 patients. The verifier achieved 100% exact-set accuracy in a 6,620-claim corruption benchmark. In a 24-case pilot, GPT-5.6 Sol reproduced 72/72 prespecified atomic claims, and the frozen verifier recovered 24/24 expected conditions. During controlled degradation, ROC AUC declined from 0.899 to 0.500 while verification accuracy remained 1.000. External MGMT discrimination was weak (ROC AUC 0.543). Conclusions: Verifiability can be engineered and evaluated independently of predictive performance. LLMs may structure explanations, while final evidence-consistency checking remains deterministic.

infographic.key_insight: The study shows that biomedical AI explanations can be made machine-verifiable by linking each claim to explicit radiomic evidence, separate from prediction quality.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could improve trust and auditability of AI-assisted brain tumor imaging reports by making statements traceable to patient-specific data.
method: Aligned UPenn-GBM radiomics with de novo CaPTk features from standardized MRI and expert segmentations.
Built a neuro-semantic evidence ledger across 1,728 MRI features from T1, T1GD, T2, and FLAIR across three tumor regions.
Tested deterministic claim verification, controlled degradation, and an LLM-based claim extraction pilot.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the benchmark, semantic-state agreement was moderate overall (median 0.786, weighted kappa 0.709), the verifier reached 100% exact-set accuracy on 6,620 corrupted claims, and verification stayed 1.000 even as prediction AUC dropped from 0.899 to 0.500.
infographic.watch_item: The framework verifies whether claims match available evidence, but it does not guarantee strong clinical prediction performance or broadly generalizable external accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Evidence-Bound Reasoning: Neuro-Semantic Verification of Biomedical AI in Glioblastoma Radiogenomics

title: Efficient Multi-Granularity Knowledge Transfer for Radiology Report Generation
authors: Xubin Zhong, Zheyu Zhang, Wenjian Qin, Ning Wen
abstract: Radiology report generation can automatically generate clinical descriptions from X-ray images, thereby significantly improving the efficiency of radiologists. This task is challenging because it requires medical knowledge to accurately identify diseases and describe them in a professional manner. However, existing methods often overlook the importance of enhancing medical knowledge in describing pivotal areas, a capability that requires models to effectively extract and aggregate knowledge at multiple levels of granularity. Accordingly, we herein propose a novel and compact Efficient Multi-Granularity Knowledge Transfer (\textbf{EMGKT}) method to address the above issues. First, we encode global knowledge embeddings using a medical vision-language model, which provides contextual medical knowledge. Moreover, we devise a novel Fine-Grained Knowledge Distillation (FGKD) training task which efficiently extract fine-grained knowledge. Specifically, the FGKD training task contains teacher embeddings and student embeddings. Teacher embeddings are encoded using extra priors; while student embeddings are learned from the teacher embeddings through knowledge distillation. During inference, the student embeddings are used to enhance fine-grained knowledge while the teacher embeddings are discarded, resulting in negligible computational costs and no need for extra priors. Finally, we further develop a mixture of disease diagnosis expert classifiers to enhance knowledge extraction. The classifiers are initialized using disease embeddings and are modeled as different experts to address various granularity features. Notably, \textbf{EMGKT} can be efficiently applied to most existing methods. Extensive experiments are conducted on two widely-used public datasets and various baselines, which demonstrates the effectiveness and transferability of \textbf{EMGKT}.

infographic.key_insight: EMGKT improves radiology report generation by transferring medical knowledge at multiple granularity levels, combining global context with fine-grained distillation and expert disease classifiers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach aims to help models produce more accurate, clinically styled X-ray reports, potentially reducing reporting workload for radiologists.
method: Encodes global medical knowledge embeddings with a vision-language model for contextual understanding.
Uses Fine-Grained Knowledge Distillation to learn student embeddings from teacher embeddings, dropping extra priors at inference for low overhead.
Adds a mixture of disease diagnosis expert classifiers initialized from disease embeddings to capture different feature granularities.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was evaluated on two widely used public datasets against multiple baselines, and the abstract reports improved effectiveness and transferability.
infographic.watch_item: Reported gains depend on dataset quality and integration into existing pipelines; real-world performance may vary across scanners, hospitals, and report styles.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Multi-Granularity Knowledge Transfer for Radiology Report Generation

title: The Predictability Bias of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning in Medical Imaging
authors: Fabian Drexel, Bernhard Kainz, Jakob N. Kather, Daniel Rueckert, Lisa C. Adams, Keno K. Bressem
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn by predicting teacher representations of masked regions from visible context. Point prediction summarizes the conditional target distribution and cannot reproduce variation that the context does not resolve. We call this constraint predictability bias. In computed tomography (CT), recurrent anatomy is predictable from context, whereas the sporadic, localized pathology that determines clinical interpretation often is not. We introduce TAP-JEPA, a ViT-B/3D trained on 113,611 CT volumes that is competitive with state-of-the-art encoders (COLIPRI, Merlin, VoxelFM) in scan-level classification. We then audit the learned predictive pathway by replaying the exact masking, teacher, and predictor computations used during training. Prediction lowers the mean Skill (prevalence-normalized average precision) from 0.388 to 0.271 for pathology, but only from 0.921 to 0.873 for anatomy. Along the teacher direction, separating pathology from matched control regions in the same organ, prediction moves pathology 34.7% toward the controls and controls 13.6% toward pathology, with larger shifts farther from visible context. Replacing visible matched-control representations increases surrounding-target prediction loss more than fully replacing pathology representations across four pathology categories. Downstream, removing all final-layer pathology tokens reduces the decision margin by at most 0.45% in four of seven scan-level probes. Together, these results show that contextual predictability is not a sufficient proxy for clinical relevance in medical representation learning. Training objectives should therefore retain diagnostic features regardless of their predictability from surrounding anatomy.

infographic.key_insight: Predictive self-supervision in CT tends to preserve predictable anatomy better than diagnostically important but context-dependent pathology, creating a "predictability bias."
infographic.clinical_relevance: For medical imaging models, being easy to predict from surrounding anatomy is not the same as being clinically useful, so training goals should protect sparse pathology signals.
method: Trained TAP-JEPA, a ViT-B/3D joint-embedding predictive model, on 113,611 CT volumes.
Audited the model by replaying the exact masking, teacher, and predictor steps used in training.
Compared prediction effects on anatomy vs pathology using scan-level classification, Skill, teacher-direction shifts, and downstream probe margins.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across CT evaluation, prediction reduced mean Skill much more for pathology than anatomy (0.388→0.271 vs 0.921→0.873), and the model was competitive with COLIPRI, Merlin, and VoxelFM on scan-level classification.
infographic.watch_item: These findings come from CT data and model-specific audits, so the size of the bias may differ across modalities, datasets, and masking/training choices.
infographic.paper_title: The Predictability Bias of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning in Medical Imaging

title: Quantifying Volumetric Risk: Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction for 3D Medical Image Segmentation
authors: Shadi Alijani, Fereshteh Aghaee Meibodi, Homayoun Najjaran
abstract: Reliable volumetric segmentation is critical for clinical diagnostics, yet foundation models such as MedSAM remain deterministic and lack calibrated uncertainty under distribution shift. Existing conformal prediction methods offer statistical guarantees but are frequently applied in 2D and assume symmetric error distributions, so they do not capture the class-specific biases that arise in 3D multi-class segmentation. We propose Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction (CA-WCP), which combines latent-space density-ratio weighting for covariate shift with directional quantiles for the lower and upper volume bounds, and scales each bound by a class-specific asymmetry factor derived from validation-set false-positive and false-negative rates. We prove that CA-WCP retains the weighted-exchangeability marginal coverage guarantee for every class, and we evaluate it on 3D brain tumor segmentation (BraTS 2020) and on a synthetic multi-organ CT benchmark constructed under covariate shift. On both benchmarks the 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval for the observed coverage of CA-WCP contains the nominal 90\% level for every semantic class, while interval width is reduced by 8--14\% relative to symmetric weighted conformal prediction. We further encode the calibrated intervals into structured prompts for a multimodal large language model to produce uncertainty-conditioned radiology reports, linking distribution-shift-aware uncertainty quantification to interpretable clinical communication.

infographic.key_insight: CA-WCP makes 3D segmentation uncertainty more reliable by using class-specific asymmetric bounds and shift-aware weighting instead of a single symmetric interval.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could improve how volumetric tumor or organ segmentation uncertainty is communicated in radiology workflows, especially when models face distribution shift.
method: Uses latent-space density-ratio weighting to handle covariate shift.
Builds directional lower and upper volume bounds with conformal prediction.
Adjusts each class by false-positive/false-negative asymmetry factors from validation data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on BraTS 2020 brain tumor segmentation and a synthetic multi-organ CT shift benchmark; the abstract reports 95% Clopper-Pearson coverage intervals containing the nominal 90% level for every class and 8-14% narrower intervals than symmetric weighted conformal prediction.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on representative validation data and carefully estimated shift weights, so performance may degrade if these inputs are inaccurate or if deployment shifts beyond the calibration setting.
infographic.paper_title: Quantifying Volumetric Risk: Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction for 3D Medical Image Segmentation

title: Multi-Objective Aligned Small Language Model Framework for SUD Patient Dialogue Generation
authors: Thushara Manjari Naduvilakandy, Hyeju Jang, Mohammad Al Hasan
abstract: Substance Use Disorder (SUD) counseling requires patient responses that reflect underlying cognitive states such as beliefs, coping strategies, and readiness for change. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent text, they often fail to produce cognitively coherent and clinically realistic patient behavior, especially under ethical and data-scarce clinical settings. Moreover, deploying frontier-scale LLMs in healthcare applications presents practical challenges including high computational cost, latency, privacy concerns, and limited deployability in resource-constrained environments, motivating the need for cognitively aligned small language models (SLMs). We propose a cognitively grounded framework for SUD patient dialogue generation that explicitly models and aligns latent cognitive components with patient histories and counselor questions. Our pipeline consists of two stages: cognitive component detection and cognitive component-aligned dialogue generation. To enable effective learning with smaller models, we combine knowledge distillation from high-capacity teacher models, preference optimization from human-annotations, and attention-guided reward shaping. Extensive evaluations using automatic scores like BERTScore, ROUGE, METEOR and BLEU, and LLM-as-judge hit-metrics against both human and teacher-model references show that cognitively informed fine-tuning substantially improves cognitive realization and alignment over a generic instruction-tuned baselines and mental health domain specific SLMs, with particularly strong gains for open-ended cognitive components.

infographic.key_insight: A cognitively grounded small-language-model framework can generate more realistic SUD patient dialogue by aligning responses with latent patient states like beliefs, coping strategies, and readiness for change.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support more clinically coherent, privacy-conscious, and deployable dialogue systems for counseling workflows in resource-constrained healthcare settings.
method: Detects cognitive components from patient history and counselor questions
Uses knowledge distillation, preference optimization, and attention-guided reward shaping
Generates dialogue aligned to the detected cognitive state rather than generic responses
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements across BERTScore, ROUGE, METEOR, BLEU, and LLM-as-judge hit metrics versus generic instruction-tuned baselines and mental-health SLMs, with especially strong gains for open-ended cognitive components.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is reported from automatic and LLM-based metrics in an abstract; real-world clinical safety, robustness, and patient impact still need prospective validation.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-Objective Aligned Small Language Model Framework for SUD Patient Dialogue Generation

title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Model with Heterogeneous Evidence Integration for Clinical Prognosis
authors: Hamza Shafiq, Jialu Tang, Ting Dang, Jun Hu, Aaqib Saeed
abstract: Clinical prognosis requires integrating structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context. We introduce PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model that combines per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of longitudinal ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank. Retrieval operates in representation space: the model receives mean-pooled embeddings of similar training-cohort encounters, while no individual retrieved record enters the prompt. On the 1,443-task MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM achieves AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality. These results use a 96-hour pre-arrival window unavailable to reported baselines. With benchmark-window inputs only, PRISM reaches 0.8895 AUROC, compared with 0.8937 for UniPACT and 0.8889 for MDS-ED. A matched-input compact fusion model using the same five evidence streams and frozen encoders reaches 0.7652 AUROC, versus 0.9092 for PRISM. Replacing numerical EHR encoding with text serialization reduces AUROC by 3.66 points; removing pre-arrival history reduces it by 1.97 points; and zeroing retrieval reduces it by 0.99 points. Genuine retrieval outperforms random-neighbor retrieval by 0.97 macro-average points, although a paired task-level sign test does not establish a uniform advantage (p=0.067). On the external MC-MED cohort, supervised fine-tuning reaches 0.8611 AUROC, compared with 0.8227 for locally trained gradient boosting and 0.7841 for source-only PRISM. These results support structure-aware multimodal integration and supervised external adaptation.

infographic.key_insight: PRISM is a retrieval-augmented multimodal model that fuses structured EHR data, ECG history, and cohort memory to improve clinical prognosis prediction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It may help forecast outcomes such as diagnosis, deterioration, ICU admission, and mortality by integrating multiple evidence streams rather than relying on a single data source.
method: Encodes per-feature numerical EHR data and recency-weighted longitudinal ECG signals.
Retrieves similar cohort information in embedding space using a population memory bank without exposing individual records in the prompt.
Combines heterogeneous evidence with frozen encoders for prognosis prediction and external adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM reported AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality, with the strongest external cohort result reaching 0.8611 AUROC after fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: Performance comparisons may be sensitive to the 96-hour pre-arrival window and benchmark-specific inputs, so real-world generalization and implementation should be validated carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Model with Heterogeneous Evidence Integration for Clinical Prognosis

title: CoBe: A Benchmark For Conversational Counterfactual Text Editing
authors: Arvind Raghavan, Inwoo Hwang, Shreyas Havaldar, Kai-Zhan Lee, Aurghya Maiti, Yushu Pan
abstract: Counterfactual text editing is the ability to revise a given text in light of a hypothetical change while preserving facts not causally affected by that change. When asked what would have happened if a doctor had not recommended surgery, the model output should retain the patient's medical history and modify only the consequences of the decision. This requires causal understanding: a model must determine, without being explicitly instructed to, what events are affected by the hypothetical change and what should remain fixed. This skill is central to human reasoning, especially in safety-critical domains like healthcare or law. By contrast, the task of associational text generation merely generates text statistically associated with the altered condition. In the medical example, an associational response might make the patient's symptoms less severe because milder cases correlate with no surgery. Such responses produce a plausible scenario, but not the counterfactual version of the given one. Prior counterfactual-text datasets do not clearly separate these modes of reasoning. We introduce the Counterfactual Benchmark (CoBe), a testbed for models' zero-shot ability to counterfactually edit a given textual scenario when prompted to do so in a conversationally natural way. CoBe contains 2000 questions spanning healthcare, science and engineering, business, and everyday scenarios. We test a suite of frontier and smaller models, with frontier systems achieving an average score of $58.05\%$. Our findings indicate that models frequently default to associational generation rather than preserving the causal structure of the original scenario. Moreover, performance does not scale consistently with either model size or output token length, suggesting that the failure may reflect model training objectives rather than insufficient model capacity.

infographic.key_insight: CoBe shows that models often rewrite scenarios associatively instead of preserving unchanged facts when asked to make counterfactual edits.
infographic.clinical_relevance: In healthcare-facing AI, preserving causal medical details while changing only the hypothetical outcome is essential for reliable, safety-sensitive communication.
method: Built CoBe, a benchmark of 2,000 conversational counterfactual editing questions.
Covers healthcare, science and engineering, business, and everyday scenarios.
Evaluates zero-shot model behavior on whether edits keep causal structure intact.
infographic.evidence_signal: Frontier models averaged 58.05% on the benchmark, and performance did not scale consistently with model size or output length.
infographic.watch_item: A key implementation concern is that fluent outputs may still be wrong if the model changes unaffected facts, so human review is needed for high-stakes use.
infographic.paper_title: CoBe: A Benchmark For Conversational Counterfactual Text Editing
